(CNN) -- A college student who survived a boat sinking with four others said Monday that a safety officer who died on their boat was a hero for staying behind and pushing him out. Texas A&M student Steven Guy, left, and instructor Steve Conway talk about their boat capsizing. Steven Guy, a Texas A&M University sailor, said Roger Stone saved him and another sailor by helping them to safety. "He is my hero," Guy said. "He saved me. If it wasn't for him, I would not be here." The group never saw Stone after he pushed the two men out of a hatch in the boat, the mariners said. Stone, the boat's second safety officer, was found dead by the Coast Guard on Sunday afternoon. The two men said they spent a day in open water after their vessel sank in the Gulf of Mexico. The survivors -- four university students and a safety officer -- told the Coast Guard they were forced off their sailboat after it took on water and capsized early Saturday. The five survivors were found and airlifted to land around 2 a.m. Sunday, the Coast Guard said. The group had to get out of the rapidly sinking sailboat so quickly, they could get only four safety vests for five people, safety officer Steve Conway said Monday. They had to huddle in the water to keep each other afloat, he said.  Watch the rescue and see Conway describe the ordeal » . "With five people and four life jackets, we had to watch the person without the life jacket closely," he said. "These young men did a tremendous job. They pulled themselves through. They had a fierce will to live." R. Bowen Loftin, CEO  and vice president of Texas A&M at Galveston, expressed condolences to the Stone family in a letter posted along with status updates on the school's Web site. "We hope they can take some comfort in knowing all five survivors of this tragic accident credit Mr. Stone with heroic efforts that were instrumental in making possible their survival," Loftin said on the site. "We now know that Roger Stone died a hero in the classic sense of the word." Conway said that as the group huddled in the water, they saw rescue jets go by three times before they were spotted. "It is really discouraging when a plane comes out and flies over and leaves," he said. Coast Guard Lt. Justo Rivera, who was flying the aircraft that rescued the men, told CNN affiliate KHOU that a flashlight helped save them. While conducting search patterns, Coast Guard members spotted the light through their night vision goggles, Rivera said. It was being held by one of the men. He said that because the Coast Guard was searching such a vast area, the flashlight was "instrumental" in the rescue. "It's your proverbial needle in a haystack," Rivera told KHOU. During the 26-hour wait, the group was nibbled by curious reed fish and circled by a fish with triangular fin that extended from the water like a shark's fin. "They bumped up against us and kind of nibbled on our clothes," Conway said. "You don't know how big the thing is and how hungry it is. I was always aware of the risk of sharks." The group's sailboat, named the Cynthia Woods, was one of about two dozen boats heading from Galveston, Texas, to Veracruz, Mexico, for the annual Veracruz Regatta race, which began Friday.

outputs.L1:
(CNN) — A college student who survived a boat sinking with four others said Monday that a safety officer who died aboard their vessel was a hero for staying behind and pushing him to safety.

Texas A&M student Steven Guy and instructor Steve Conway spoke about the capsizing of their boat. Guy, a Texas A&M University sailor, said Roger Stone saved him and another sailor by helping them escape.

“He is my hero,” Guy said. “He saved me. If it wasn’t for him, I would not be here.”

The mariners said they never saw Stone again after he pushed the two men out through a hatch in the boat. Stone, the vessel’s second safety officer, was found dead by the Coast Guard on Sunday afternoon.

The two men said they spent a day in open water after their vessel sank in the Gulf of Mexico. The survivors — four university students and a safety officer — told the Coast Guard they were forced off their sailboat after it took on water and capsized early Saturday. The five survivors were found and airlifted to land around 2 a.m. Sunday, the Coast Guard said.

Safety officer Steve Conway said Monday that the group had to escape the rapidly sinking sailboat so quickly that they were able to retrieve only four life vests for five people. They had to huddle together in the water to keep one another afloat, he said.

“With five people and four life jackets, we had to watch the person without the life jacket closely,” Conway said. “These young men did a tremendous job. They pulled themselves through. They had a fierce will to live.”

R. Bowen Loftin, CEO and vice president of Texas A&M at Galveston, expressed condolences to the Stone family in a letter posted alongside status updates on the school’s website.

“We hope they can take some comfort in knowing all five survivors of this tragic accident credit Mr. Stone with heroic efforts that were instrumental in making possible their survival,” Loftin said on the site. “We now know that Roger Stone died a hero in the classic sense of the word.”

Conway said that while the group huddled in the water, they saw rescue jets pass overhead three times before they were finally spotted.

“It is really discouraging when a plane comes out and flies over and leaves,” he said.

Coast Guard Lt. Justo Rivera, who was flying the aircraft that rescued the men, told CNN affiliate KHOU that a flashlight helped save them. While conducting search patterns, Coast Guard members spotted the light through their night-vision goggles, Rivera said. It was being held by one of the men.

Because the Coast Guard was searching such a vast area, Rivera said, the flashlight was “instrumental” in the rescue.

“It’s your proverbial needle in a haystack,” Rivera told KHOU.

During the 26-hour wait, the group was nibbled by curious reed fish and circled by a fish with a triangular fin that extended from the water like a shark’s fin.

“They bumped up against us and kind of nibbled on our clothes,” Conway said. “You don’t know how big the thing is and how hungry it is. I was always aware of the risk of sharks.”

The group’s sailboat, named the *Cynthia Woods*, was one of about two dozen vessels traveling from Galveston, Texas, to Veracruz, Mexico, for the annual Veracruz Regatta race, which began Friday.
outputs.L2:
(CNN) — One of five people who lived through a sailboat sinking said Monday that a safety officer who died aboard the vessel acted heroically by remaining behind and helping push him to safety.

Texas A&M student Steven Guy and instructor Steve Conway spoke about the capsizing of their boat. Guy, a sailor at Texas A&M University, said Roger Stone helped save both him and another sailor by getting them out of danger.

“He is my hero,” Guy said. “He saved me. If it wasn't for him, I would not be here.”

The surviving mariners said they never saw Stone again after he pushed the two men through a hatch and out of the boat. Stone, who served as the vessel’s second safety officer, was found dead by the Coast Guard on Sunday afternoon.

The two men said they spent roughly a day in the open waters of the Gulf of Mexico after their boat went down. The survivors — four college students and one safety officer — told the Coast Guard they had to abandon their sailboat after it began taking on water and overturned early Saturday.

According to the Coast Guard, the five survivors were located and flown back to land at about 2 a.m. Sunday.

Safety officer Steve Conway said Monday that the sailboat was sinking so fast that the group was able to grab only four life jackets for five people. To stay above water, he said, they had to remain close together and support one another.

“With five people and four life jackets, we had to watch the person without the life jacket closely,” Conway said. “These young men did a tremendous job. They pulled themselves through. They had a fierce will to live.”

R. Bowen Loftin, CEO and vice president of Texas A&M at Galveston, offered sympathy to Stone’s family in a letter posted on the school’s website along with updates about the incident.

“We hope they can take some comfort in knowing all five survivors of this tragic accident credit Mr. Stone with heroic efforts that were instrumental in making possible their survival,” Loftin wrote. “We now know that Roger Stone died a hero in the classic sense of the word.”

Conway said that while the group stayed clustered together in the water, rescue aircraft passed over them three times before finally spotting them.

“It is really discouraging when a plane comes out and flies over and leaves,” he said.

Coast Guard Lt. Justo Rivera, who was aboard the aircraft that eventually rescued the men, told CNN affiliate KHOU that a flashlight played a key role in their survival. Rivera said that during the search, Coast Guard members noticed the light through night-vision goggles. One of the men was holding it.

Because rescuers were covering an enormous search area, Rivera said, the flashlight was “instrumental” in locating them.

“It’s your proverbial needle in a haystack,” Rivera told KHOU.

During the 26 hours they waited in the water, the group was bitten lightly by curious reed fish and was also circled by a fish with a triangular fin sticking above the surface, resembling a shark fin.

“They bumped up against us and kind of nibbled on our clothes,” Conway said. “You don’t know how big the thing is and how hungry it is. I was always aware of the risk of sharks.”

Their sailboat, the Cynthia Woods, had been among about two dozen vessels traveling from Galveston, Texas, to Veracruz, Mexico, as part of the annual Veracruz Regatta, which started Friday.

*By [Your Name]*

A Texas A&M University student survived hours in the Gulf of Mexico after the university sailboat *Cynthia Woods* sank during an offshore race, an ordeal that ended with a dramatic U.S. Coast Guard rescue and renewed attention on the bravery of a safety officer who helped save others before losing his own life.

Authorities and survivors credited safety officer Roger Stone with helping others escape the sinking boat. Stone, an experienced sailor and safety official, has been remembered for actions that crew members say gave students a chance to survive. He did not make it out.

The Coast Guard launched a search-and-rescue operation after the boat was reported missing. Crews searched a wide area of the Gulf by air and sea before locating survivors. Rescue personnel pulled Guy and other crew members from the water after they had spent hours awaiting help.

For the students, the rescue marked the end of a nightmare. For the Texas A&M community, it brought both relief and grief — relief that several crew members survived, and grief over the loss of Stone, whose conduct in the emergency was widely described as heroic.

The sinking of the *Cynthia Woods* prompted investigations and safety reviews, including scrutiny of the boat’s condition and what caused it to go down so quickly. But for those who survived, the story remains deeply personal: a sudden disaster at sea, a desperate fight to stay alive, and the actions of a safety officer who put the lives of students ahead of his own.

Stone’s legacy has endured among Texas A&M sailors and the broader university community as an example of courage under extreme pressure. The Coast Guard rescue, meanwhile, underscored the urgency and complexity of offshore search operations — and the difference those efforts can make when minutes and miles separate survival from tragedy.
